title: "What is the point in learning this?" - Can AI help us answer this question?
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton, a self-described explicit-instruction advocate, concedes that explicit teaching often fails to convey why a procedure matters, so students do not care enough to attend. He offers four ways to spend a few minutes establishing purpose: connect prior, present and future knowledge with a flow diagram; share hinterland stories; use genuine real-life contexts rather than contrived ones; and introduce a short 'headache' in Dan Meyer's headache-aspirin style. He then tests ChatGPT and Claude with a structured prompt for fractions, pie charts and quadratic graphs, concluding that AI produces useful ideas but needs teacher judgement. Barton's move is to reconcile explicit instruction with student motivation by making purpose a short, planned part of teaching.
points: Good explanations are wasted when students see no purpose, so a few minutes of purpose-setting buys attention.
Hinterland stories exploit the fact that narrative is easier to remember, citing Willingham.
Contrived real-world contexts backfire; genuine uses such as cybersecurity primes or sports averages are better.
A headache of two minutes at most, followed by a crisp I Do, differs from prolonged discovery struggle.
AI can generate purpose ideas in seconds but its suggestions must be filtered by the teacher.
quotes: I watch many lessons each week in which the teacher delivers a good explanation and worked example of a procedure, but their efforts are largely wasted because the kids just don’t care. If they don’t care, then students are unlikely to pay attention and put in the effort required to grasp a new idea. And why should they care? If we don’t convey the purpose of the ideas we teach them, we should not expect students to buy in.

What foundations is this new idea built upon, and what doors will it open in the future? If we can show students that their past efforts have put them in the perfect position to learn the new idea and that if they put in the effort required to master it, they will be able to access many other exciting ideas, we might get their buy-in.

Maths teachers have a rich history to draw upon. Every technique our students need to learn was born from a need in a time gone by, and that cast of characters involved in their creation is worth sharing.
Daniel Willingham describes stories as being psychologically privileged as humans have evolved to enjoy and retain the narrative structure.

But if you can share a genuine real-life context with students they can relate to, it can help convey the purpose of the idea we are about to teach. The use of prime numbers in cybersecurity or averages to compare players in sports are two examples that tend to work well.

An important point here is that the struggle is short. 2 minutes at most. In my eyes, this makes it distinct from those lessons where students wrestle with a problem they don’t yet have the tools to solve for many minutes, with the teacher slowly facilitating their path to the solution. No, I am talking about a couple of minutes of pain, followed by a clear, concise I Do.

Once you have the prompt, you can generate similar ideas for any lesson you are teaching in less than 5 seconds. So long as you are willing to spend a few minutes reading the responses and thinking about the most suitable for that topic and your particular class, you have a tool that could save you time and help you do your job better.
